The Big Story 

Hegseth backs Trump on banning media outlets

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said on Friday that he “fully supports” President Trump’s decision to ban CNN, MS Now and Politico from the White House, claiming those outlets “endangered” U.S. service members with “false stories.” 

AP Photo/Mark Schiefelbein

“The Department of War fully supports President Trump’s decision to kick CNN, MSN̶B̶C̶NOW and Politico to the curb so they can publish their Fake News from outside the White House,” Hegseth said in a statement on Friday.  

 

“We are grateful these outlets already chose to self-deport from the Pentagon,” the defense secretary added. “They endangered our troops with false stories, leaks, and trafficked in fiction and lies about the President, our Warriors and their mission.” 

 

Trump said the ban is set to be in effect immediately, happening “as a result of their constant ‘reporting’ FAKE NEWS!”

 

“It’s really just cumulative stories over the last two years. You get sick of it,” the president told reporters at the White House, adding that more news outlets could be banned in the future. 

 

Hegseth’s endorsement of Trump’s decision comes as the defense secretary has imposed his own media restrictions since taking the helm at the Pentagon.

 

His policies have barred journalists from large portions of the department from walking freely without an escort and have prevented reporters from retaining their Pentagon credentials unless they agree to publish only unclassified information approved by current U.S. defense officials. 

 

Hegseth and his allies have argued those measures are necessary to safeguard critical national security information and prevent unauthorized leaks. 

 

Those opposed to the policies, including news outlets and press freedom advocates, have argued that the Pentagon is stymying independent reporting. 

 

Trump’s Friday ban was panned by both CNN and Politico, stating they will defend their First Amendment rights. 

 

The ban was also criticized by some Fox News contributors, arguing it sets a bad precedent and could backfire in the long-term.

data.title: Hawley invites Flock, Axon, other surveillance tech CEOs to testify
data.description:
Sen. Josh Hawley (R-Mo.) invited the CEOs of Flock Safety and other prominent AI-powered surveillance camera manufacturers to testify before the upper chamber’s Judiciary Subcommittee on Crime and Counterterrorism next week.

Hawley, the subcommittee’s chair, wrote on social media Friday that he “invited the CEOs of Flock Safety, Axon, Motorola and Verkada to testify in front of my committee NEXT WEEK.” Each of the companies the senator listed produce AI-based automatic license plate recognition (ALPR) cameras — which have been scrutinized on both sides of the aisle.

“Americans deserve answers,” Hawley added. 

The Republican’s letters invited Flock’s Garrett Langley, Axon’s Rick Smith, Motorola Solutions’ Greg Brown and Verkada’s Filip Kaliszan to testify on Sept. 23 as part of his investigation into privacy concerns surrounding these ALPRs — which several jurisdictions have removed following reports of data misuse.

The Hill has reached out to the four companies for comment; Flock Axon and Motorola Solutions did not immediately respond to the request.

A Verkada spokesperson told the Hill that Kaliszan is “unable to attend next week’s hearing.”

“We are in communication with the Subcommittee and are providing information to assist Chairman Hawley and Ranking Member Durbin as they prepare for the hearing,” the spokesperson said. “As we’ve explained to the Subcommittee, none of our customers can search a national Verkada network – because none exists. Our customers can only access the data in their own systems.”

The senator has cited concerns with these companies’ citizen data collection and retention policies, as Flock cameras — for example — share information across a national network.

In a previous letter to Langley, announcing his investigation into Flock, Hawley cited St. Charles County Police Department — who terminated its contract with the surveillance camera company after an audit revealing an officer used its database for personal reasons. 

Over 170 contracts have been cancelled with Flock alone, according to anti-surveillance group DeFlock.

Hawley’s first letter also referenced a case in Milwaukee, where prosecutors charged a police officer for allegedly using Flock’s database to search his girlfriend’s license plate 124 times and her former boyfriend’s plate 55 times. The officer entered “investigation” as his reasoning behind each search, but the system never flagged these searches.

On Sept. 3, Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) unveiled the Flock-Off Act in the House, which would block the use of federal funding for ALPRs and biometric surveillance cameras. 

Massie said in a press release that cities and police departments have used the technology to turn “their communities into a version of ‘1984,’” George Orwell’s famous dystopian novel.

The issue has divided key figures within the GOP, with President Trump voicing his support for the technology Sunday.

“No, I sort of like [Flock cameras] because of that, because of law enforcement. But some people don’t. They think it’s an infringement,” the president said, adding, “I like them.”

data.title: Trump officially signs Russia sanctions bill into law
data.description:
President Trump officially signed the Russia sanctions bill into law Friday, which authorizes further sanctions and tariffs against Russia amid the Kremlin’s ongoing conflict with Ukraine.

The bill — championed and named after late Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.)  — calls for the president to impose tariffs of up to 100 percent on the top five purchasers of Russian energy, or on countries helping Russia evade sanctions — even extending current sanctions on Iran.

Drafters of the bill, Graham and Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.), intended for the sanctions to target resources Russian President Vladimir Putin needed to continue Moscow’s war effort.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky thanked the president on social media for signing the “critically important” legislation.

“I thank all the senators and members of the House of Representatives who supported it. The best way to honor Lindsey’s memory will be to implement the provisions of this law fully and swiftly,” he wrote. “And the best reward for everyone helping us put pressure on Russia to end its war will be peace. Peace – and an end to all the problems and challenges this war has brought.”

The bill passed both chambers with large margins, but in the House, Democratic opposition worried about provisions that handed over tariff authorities to the president.

“Life is way too expensive in the United States of America. Why in the world would this Congress or the People’s House give this president unfettered authority to visit more tariffs on the world that will have an adverse economic impact on the American people?” said House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.), explaining his “no” vote. “I can’t do it.”

Trump stalled the bill for months, arguing that he wanted greater flexibility to negotiate with Putin. In September, special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, Trump’s son-in-law, visited Moscow and Kyiv.

Witkoff said the U.S. is confident that trilateral talks will result in a “good resolution” to the Ukraine war after a weekend long ceasefire was called for their visit. 

The conflict, however, has reignited since peace talks, with Russia hitting targets in Kyiv and other major cities earlier this week, according to Reuters. Ukrainian officials told the outlet that over 20 were injured in the strikes.

data.title: Pentagon's count leaves out some deaths in Middle East during Iran war
data.description:
The Pentagon’s public database left out two deaths of U.S. service members deployed in the Middle East during the war against Iran, who took part in missions unrelated to the conflict in the Middle East. 

Maj. Sorffly Davius, who served in the 42nd Infantry Division at Camp Buehring, Kuwait, died of “undetermined causes” on March 6 this year. The release announcing his death said he deployed to Kuwait in the summer of 2025 in support of Operation Spartan Shield. 

Sgt. Devin Seibel, who was assigned to the Air Ambulance Company, 2nd Battalion, 4th Combat Aviation Brigade, Fort Carson, Colo., died on May 31 in Erbil Airbase, Iraq, during a “training-related incident,” the Pentagon said in a June press release. Seibel, whose death is under investigation, deployed in support of Operation Inherent Resolve.

Their deaths are not included in the Pentagon’s Defense Casualty Analysis System (DCAS), which came under fire earlier this year for briefly excluding names of several U.S. service members who were killed because of Iranian military attacks. 

Eighteen service members have been killed since the U.S. war with Iran began in late February — including in hostile and non-hostile action — and more than 800 have been injured, the DCAS database said as of Friday. 

The Washington Post first reported Friday on Davius and Seibel’s exclusion from the DCAS and that at least another two service members have died in the Middle East during the Iran conflict who are not included in the database, citing five U.S. officials, bringing the death toll from the war to a minimum of 22. 

A sixth U.S. official told the news outlet that 23 service members have died since Feb. 28, which is when the U.S. military kicked off Operation Epic Fury, the Trump administration’s name for the war against Iran. This source added that three U.S. contractors who were based in the U.S. Central Command (Centcom) region have died since the conflict began. 

The Pentagon’s press office did not respond to The Hill’s request for comment. 

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth lashed out at the news outlet, calling the report “DISGUSTING and FAKE.”  

“Shame on the Washington Post — they’re worse than Iranian state media,” the defense secretary said in a post. 

Earlier this year, the Pentagon’s death toll database came under fire from Congressional Democrats after names of four U.S. service members who were killed during renewed Iranian strikes were temporarily removed from DCAS. The department later restored their deaths into the database. 

Fourteen deaths are listed in the DCAS under the category Operation Epic Fury as of Friday. Four other deaths are listed in another section dubbed “Overseas Operations,” which coincided with the July 7 ceasefire date between the U.S. and Iran. 

Senate Democrats, who all sit on the Senate Armed Services Committee, pressed Hegseth in late July to provide a “full and accurate accounting” of the U.S. service member casualties during the war with Iran, adding that the Pentagon’s DCAS “has reported inconsistent casualty figures, raising additional questions about the transparency and reliability of the Department’s public reporting and statements.” 

In the lower chamber, Democrats on the House Armed Services Committee (HASC) have sent multiple congressional Requests for Information (RFI) asking the Pentagon about the discrepancy between the casualties listed on DCAS and the actual figures, two sources familiar with the requests told The Hill on Friday. 

The Pentagon has not responded to these lawmakers, sources said.  

Rep. Adam Smith (D-Wash.), the HASC ranking member, said Friday that he is “aware” of the reports that the actual number of U.S. service members who died while backing operations in the Middle East is likely higher than previously disclosed by the Pentagon. 

“Whether these additional deaths were the direct result of hostile fire or were non-combat related, they died while serving our country and each loss is a tragedy,” Smith said in a statement, adding that the department “owes” it to Congress and the American public to be “more transparent about the impacts and true cost of this war.” 

Rep. Jason Crow (D-Colo.), a former Army Ranger and HASC member, accused Hegseth on Friday of “covering up” the deaths of U.S. service members and contractors. “

“It’s a betrayal of the men & women who have served and sacrificed for our country,” Crow said in a post on social platform X.

The Colorado lawmaker added that he is introducing a bill, alongside other Democratic HASC members, to bar the Pentagon from “manipulating government data on troop casualties and therefore hiding the human cost of war.”

data.title: CDC director says RFK Jr. has final say
data.description:

The Big Story 

CDC director says RFK Jr. has final say

In her first interview since taking leadership of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, Erica Schwartz told Atlanta News First that she isn’t afraid to disagree with Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.

Jacquelyn Martin, Associated Press file

Schwartz emphasized that any kind of disagreement will happen behind closed doors, and she won’t publicly contradict Kennedy.  

 

“In the uniformed services, we have something called ‘but sir, but ma’am,’ which basically means you can disagree with your superiors,” Schwartz said. “Secretary Kennedy and I have worked together for five weeks now, and I can tell you there have been a few ‘but sirs’ behind closed doors.” 

 

However, Schwartz said that even if she disagrees, Kennedy is her boss and makes the final decisions. 

 

“At the end of the day, he’s the Secretary of HHS,” Schwartz said. “And at the end of the day, he’s going to make the decisions.” 

 

Schwartz’s comments mark a strong contrast with the previous CDC director Susan Monarez, who pushed back against Kennedy’s vaccine agenda and was fired after being on the job less than a month.  

 

Schwartz, deputy surgeon general in the first Trump administration and a top Coast Guard health official, has publicly supported childhood vaccines and was viewed as a highly qualified, mainstream choice who could bring stability back to CDC.  

  

But Democrats and even GOP Sen. Bill Cassidy (R-La.) expressed serious doubts about her willingness and ability to push back against Kennedy’s policies and stand up for science.   

 

Amid the country’s record-setting measles outbreak, Schwartz is facing criticism for directing the CDC to dispute four measles-associated deaths in Pennsylvania and decline to include them in the agency’s official tally of cases and deaths.  

 

The move followed public comments from Kennedy calling the reports “fabricated” and an ongoing political feud between Kennedy and Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro (D). In an Oval Office event Friday, Kennedy doubled down when asked about measles, calling the deaths “alleged.” 

 

Schwartz characterized the controversy as a technical dispute, and said CDC doesn’t yet have a standardized definition of a measles—related death. In the interview, Schwartz drew a comparison to the disputes about COVID-19 deaths. 
 
“If someone got hit by a bus, and they happened to have COVID, often that was called a COVID-related death,” Schwartz said. 

 

But Pennsylvania officials have said their definition is based on how CDC classifies other respiratory virus deaths. They won’t count it if someone obviously dies from an unrelated event, like a car crash.

data.title: GOP senator: Russian oligarch funding Trump Jr.'s party is 'corruption'
data.description:
Sen. John Curtis (R-Utah) on Friday ripped President Trump’s son, Donald Trump Jr., for letting a Russian oligarch with ties to the Kremlin pay hundreds of thousands of dollars to finance his wedding after-party in the Bahamas this year.

Curtis called the generous gift “corruption,” and pledged to say more about it in coming days.

“A Russian oligarch paid for a lavish wedding after-party for Donald Trump Jr. which to me just thinks. It’s corruption, I don’t like it,” Curtis said in a video summary of the week’s events posted on social media.

“You’ll hear more from me later on. This is a big deal,” he continued.  

Curtis touched on the subject as one of the “lows” of the week.

ProPublica broke the story on Sunday, reporting that Russian businessman, Umar Kremlev, the president of the International Boxing Association, paid to rent one of two private islands where Trump Jr. and his new wife, Bettina Trump, held three-day lavish party.

Kremlev paid for the pricey fireworks show and other expenses, according to ProPublica.

Bettina Trump confirmed in a social media post that the couple’s “dear friend Umar very generously hosted two incredible nights of celebrations” but emphasized it was “AFTER” the wedding itself, which was a private ceremony at which only family attended.

President Trump said Friday that his son paid back Kremlev for the wedding expenses and dismissed a question about whether it was appropriate to accept in the first place.

“Well, it’s totally allowed, and a lot of people have parties and all, but it’s totally allowed,” the president said. “But as I understand it, he paid him back. He didn’t want to have that, so I hear he paid him back.”

Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) criticized the arrangement earlier this week, calling it “beyond bad.”

Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.), however, declined to criticize Trump Jr. when asked about it Thursday, telling reporters he needed more information.

“I don’t know all the particulars on that. I’ve seen — or heard, I should say — some of the reporting around that. I just don’t know enough about it,” Thune said.

data.title: How do we still know so little about Thomas Crooks
data.description:
One of the highest honors of my professional life was serving as director of communications for the late Sen. Bob Dole (R-Kan.). Because of his poor childhood; his heroic actions in World War II; the three years he spent in a hospital fighting to survive his almost mortal wounds; and the innate goodness within him, I truly don’t know a human being who cared more for the suffering and disenfranchised of our nation, or who shed more real tears for them. 

As the driving force behind Washington, D.C.’s World War Two Memorial, Dole not only morphed into “America’s veteran” but he also served as a political template for how to work across the aisle to get things done for the American people — most especially, its disabled citizens. 

All of those positives and warm memories came flooding back into my mind after reading, of all things, news that the attempted Trump assassin, Thomas Crooks, used “Bob Dole” as an alias when ordering “suspicious packages.” Suddenly, Bob Dole’s name may be forever linked to a very troubled young man who killed one innocent bystander and wounded two others while attempting to assassinate Trump. 

I first became a fan of Trump while working in the Reagan White House and after reading his bestselling book “The Art of the Deal.” I honestly believed it to be one of the best “real world” business books ever written. 

Flash ahead to three days before the assassination attempt in Butler, Pa. Then a former president, Trump had been kind enough to invite me to his golf course in Jupiter, Fla., for a private breakfast and to hit the links. We spoke about golf, business and politics. 

What most stuck with me about that very special moment was how incredibly kind and genuine Trump was to everyone at his country club. Not only did he know each staff member by name, he also knew the names of their children. He joked with them, laughed with them, and bonded with them. It showed a real side of him that the American people rarely get to see because of a highly adversarial mainstream media. 

Like him or not, agree with him or not, this is a president who has been mercilessly attacked by journalists who have dubbed themselves part of what they call “the resistance.” He had the deep state of two previous administrations marshalled against him, and lawfare was used in an attempt to destroy his candidacy, imprison him or both. Far-left activist judges are still seeking to unwind or delay his policies and, in many cases, upend the will of the American people. 

After engaging in one more conversation with Trump that day in 2024, I walked past his Secret Service detail and said, “Thank you for service and please protect him.” I felt the need to say that because I knew in three days’ time, the president would be attending yet another outdoor campaign rally, in Butler, Pa. Precisely because of the ever-escalating hateful rhetoric of the far left, I did fear it could trigger an already damaged mind.

Was that the case with Thomas Crooks? That is but one of an endless series of unanswered questions regarding that fateful day.

Douglas MacKinnon is a former White House and Pentagon official.

data.title: Fox News contributors denounce Trump's ban on CNN, MSNOW, Politico
data.description:
Several contributors to Fox News on Friday offered stark criticism of President Trump’s decision to ban CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House. 

Trump announced the decision in a Friday Truth Social post, saying the ban would be “effective immediately” for those outlets, “as a result of their constant ‘reporting’ FAKE NEWS!” He suggested more outlets would be banned in the future.

Fox News Contributor Ari Fleischer was quick to respond on social media Friday, writing, “I agree with POTUS that several media outlets covering the WH are biased and unfair.”

“Banning them from the WH is not the solution. Open the pool and the briefing room to conservatives. Challenge liberal reporters. Argue and defeat them,” he stated. “Don’t ban them. Or one day they’ll ban us.”

Fox News’ Chief Political Analyst Brit Hume also wrote on social media that he “100%” agreed with a post from Jonathan Turley, a George Washington University Law School professor.

Turley called Trump’s move “terrible precedent and practice” that “would raise serious constitutional questions and undermine the country’s long-standing position as a voice for the free press.”

Hume added that if Trump “thinks this will lead to more favorable coverage, I think he’s dreaming.”

When asked in the Oval Office about the ban, Trump said he did it, “because they’re fake news. You get so tired of reading and seeing fake news.” 

“But our country has to have honest news,” he added.

The ban comes after Trump attempted to sue CNN for defamation for the outlet’s reporting on the 2020 election. He also sued the Wall Street Journal last year over its reporting on his alleged ties to the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

data.title: Republican highlights man freed from ICE custody in campaign ad
data.description:
Rep. Monica De La Cruz (R-Texas) released a campaign advertisement featuring a man she helped get released Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) custody, along with his wife —who described the U.S.’s immigration system as “broken.”

The ad, which first aired last week, shows an interview with Weslaco, Texas woman whose husband — a Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals (DACA) recipient — was detained by ICE.

The interviewee, named Stephanie, said he was freed after she reached out De La Cruz — the Texas 15th Congressional District incumbent locked in a tight race with Democratic challenger, Bobby Pulido.

“My husband and I did things the right way, but we were stuck in a broken immigration system,” Stephanie said. “We need to secure our borders to keep our families safe, but this immigration system is broken. So, we reached out to Monica de la Cruz.”

“She helped with my husband’s immigration case. I’ve voted Democrat before, but Monica puts people over politics,” the woman continued.

De La Cruz is not the first Latina Republican to break with President Trump on immigration. On Thursday, Rep. Maria Elvira Salazar (R-Fla.) — running for reelection in Florida’s 27th Congressional District — released her own campaign video accusing the president of going “too far” with his escalated immigration enforcement operations.

“The same Hispanics who helped you get to the White House in 2024 feel betrayed today,” Salazar said.

Both Salazar and De La Cruz represent predominately Hispanic districts, according to Census data.

Stephanie’s husband would not be the first person the Texas Republican has gotten out of ICE custody. In March, she escorted Antonio Gámez-Cuéllar, a teenager detained for nearly two weeks, out of an immigration detention facility to his loved ones.

“This is about our community coming together for, not only their family, but other families who are in similar situations,” De La Cruz said at the time, adding that her colleagues in Congress should work on “common sense” enforcement policies, the Texas Tribune reported.

De La Cruz faces a fierce challenge from Pulido, who gained traction within the 15th District.

An August poll from Texas Southern University’s Barbara Jordan Public Policy and Research and Survey Center reported that De La Cruz trailed Pulido by 5-points.

Cook Political Report July 16 update stated that “under normal circumstances, a district Trump carried by 18 points should not be competitive. But due to a number of unique factors” De La Cruz “faces a serious challenge from” Pulido. 

De La Cruz has ramped up campaign efforts as November approaches, both through releasing this ad and giving a speech at Trump’s Republican National Committee midterm convention.

But De La Cruz still praised Trump for his handling of the U.S. southern border, saying in her ad, “Working with President Trump, we ended the border crisis, and today that border is safer than any point in history.”

All 50 states, Washington, D.C. and Puerto Rico have applied to participate in an arrangement intended to give lower drug prices to Medicaid programs, President Trump said Friday. 

“This one thing alone should win us the midterms,” Trump told reporters in the Oval Office.

Forty states and Puerto Rico have already signed agreements, the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) said in a separate statement, and applying does not obligate states to participate. 

The administration’s “GENEROUS” model allows participating states to purchase drugs at a price aligned with those in other countries. The theory, according to the CMS, is that it will allow state Medicaid programs to benefit from fairer, more competitive pricing. 

The White House announcement comes as affordability concerns are at the forefront of voters’ concerns ahead of the November midterm elections. To try to address those concerns, Trump has cut deals with pharmaceutical companies so the cost of some drugs in the U.S. would be tied to what companies charge other wealthy countries.

But critics say the administration is merely papering over the issue, and has no real plan to deal with rising health costs— especially the ones caused when Republicans let ObamaCare’s enhanced premium subsidies expire.

The White House said participating pharmaceutical companies will provide state Medicaid programs with rebates on selected brand-name drugs to ensure the final price to Medicaid does not exceed what’s paid in other developed countries. 

More than two dozen drug companies have agreed to participate in the program, in exchange for tariff relief and exemptions from a similar pricing plan for Medicare. 

“Medicaid programs will get the best possible price for drugs, delivering better value for taxpayers and freeing up funds to give vulnerable Americans the high-quality care they deserve,” said CMS Administrator Mehmet Oz.  

The model includes hundreds of individual drugs, across virtually all major drug classes, including oncology, diabetes care, and asthma. 

The White House Council of Economic Advisers estimated the “most-favored nation” (MFN) deals in Medicaid will produce $36.6 billion in federal savings, and $27.6 billion for states.  

But Medicaid drugs are already subject to steep discounts, and many of the details of the agreements are secret, so the true impact of MFN agreements on drug costs and accessibility isn’t clear. 

 Critics said there’s little evidence that drug companies are meaningfully lowering prices at all.

“Big Pharma expects little to no financial impact from these short-term Medicaid deals. Instead, pharma companies and Trump appear to have worked together to offer minor concessions to avoid taking more meaningful action to lower prices,” Peter Maybarduk, Access to Medicines director for Public Citizen, said in a statement, calling the agreements a “charade.”
